new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemic in Malto. A syllable containing a long vowel is always stressed e.g. qēn 'guiltless'. In two consecutive syllables when both have long vowels then the last one is stressed.
new_statements.citation: Das, Sisir Kumar. 1973. Structure of Malto. Annamalainagar: Annamalai University.
new_statements.locator: p.34, section 1.6 'Stress' (PDF page 44 of the archive.org scan)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive; it is attracted to long vowels (a long-vowel syllable is stressed), and where two adjacent syllables both have long vowels the second (rightmost) carries the stress. No default position is stated for words with only short vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source does not say where stress falls in all-short-vowel words.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a phonology chapter (after intonation contours); based on Sauria-side Malto speech (Sahibganj/Godda/Hiranpur informants). The author regards Kumarbhagi as a barely distinct dialect but gives it only a lexical appendix, so application to kuma1274 is by extension, not direct observation. The kmj-specific grammar (Mahapatra 1979) notes only that vowel length is distinctive in the word-initial syllable and is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog splits Malto into Kumarbhag Paharia (kuma1274/kmj, the southern/'non-beef-eating' Malto of Pakur-Godda, incl. Mahapatra's 'Malpaharia dialect of Malto') and Sauria Paharia (saur1249/mjt). The only opened source with a stress statement, Das 1973, describes Malto from Sauria-side speakers (Hiranpur/Banjhi schools, main informant from Kusumghati, Godda) and treats 'Kumarbhagi' only in a two-page appendix (word list, no prosody), while asserting 'the difference between the two is very little... mutually understandable' (p.4) and that he 'did not notice any difference in the phonology and morphology of Malto spoken in different areas' (p.7 of intro). So the quoted statement is first-hand for Malto as a whole but its evidential base is saur1249, not kuma1274; the kmj-specific grammar (Mahapatra 1979, Malpaharia dialect) is silent on stress. Cataloguing Das under kuma1274 would count one description across two glottocodes; a sibling audit folder (saur1249) already holds Das 1973.

sources.note: Nothing. Ch. II Phonology (pp.19-59): inventory lists two junctures and notes 'The intonational contours have not been worked out' (p.19); vowel length 'significant in the initial syllable of a poly-syllabic word' (pp.21-23); sections on juncture (2.8), phonotactics, syllable (2.10), morphophonemics; no stress/accent statement anywhere. Describes the Malpaharia dialect of Malto (Pakur), i.e. the kmj side.

sources.citation: Bokade, Shubham Suresh. 2025 (Shodhganga; archive.org record says 2021). Switch Reference in Malto. PhD thesis, Indira Gandhi National Tribal University, Amarkantak.
sources.note: Nothing; ch.2 'Brief grammatical sketch' is morphosyntax only. Sauria variety (Ursa Pahar, Sahibganj) with Mal Paharia comparison.
